know-camera-obscura.hook: The camera is named after an Arabic dark room
know-camera-obscura.date: Ibn al-Haytham · Cairo, early eleventh century
lines: He set several lamps outside a small hole and showed their images stayed separate on the wall: light travels in straight lines.
know-camera-obscura.caption:
His term was the dark room. Kepler put that into Latin in 1604 as camera obscura, and the word stayed on every camera since. The experiment, several lamps outside one aperture, is what turned a curiosity noticed since antiquity into a proof about how light travels.

know-sine.hook: The word sine is a translation mistake
know-sine.date: India to Baghdad to Toledo · one word's route
lines: The Indian jya became jiba in Arabic, was misread as jayb, a fold, and a Latin translator in twelfth century Spain wrote sinus.
know-sine.caption:
Indian astronomers called the half chord jya. Carried into Arabic by sound as jiba, which means nothing, it was written without vowels and read as jayb, a real word for a fold. The Latin translator rendered the meaning he found, sinus, and English shortened it to sine. The function is Indian; the name is an accident.

know-ghubar.hook: Your digits came to Europe through the Maghrib and Spain
know-ghubar.date: Maghrib to Europe · tenth to thirteenth c.
lines: Fibonacci learned them as a boy at Bugia on the coast of what is now Algeria, where his father was a customs official.
know-ghubar.caption:
The numerals reached the Arabic speaking world from India, and split into two families of shapes. The western set, called ghubar or dust figures after the boards they were written on, is the one Europe learned: Gerbert of Aurillac met them in Catalonia in the tenth century, and Fibonacci learned them properly in Bugia.

know-cipher.hook: Zero and cipher are one Arabic word borrowed twice
know-cipher.date: Sanskrit to Arabic to Latin · one word's route
lines: Arabic sifr, meaning empty, was written into Latin two ways: zephirum became zero, and cifra became cipher.
know-cipher.caption:
The Indian mathematicians called the empty column shunya, the void. Arabic translators rendered it sifr, empty. Latin wrote that down twice, as zephirum and cifra: the first became zero, the second became cipher, which meant zero, then any digit, then a secret code. A cipher is a zero, and a zero is an emptiness, carried west in Arabic.

know-damascus-steel.hook: A Damascus sabre was dissolved in acid and held nanotubes

lines: In 2006 a group at Dresden dissolved a fragment of a seventeenth century sabre and reported carbon nanotubes, published in Nature.
know-damascus-steel.caption:
The watered blades were forged at Damascus and Isfahan, but the steel arrived as cakes of crucible metal from southern India and Sri Lanka, the material English writers called wootz. The pattern comes from bands of carbide. The technique lapsed in the eighteenth century, most likely when a particular ore stopped coming through the trade. The smiths knew which ore, which heat, and how slowly to let it cool.

know-catgut.hook: A surgeon in Cordoba closed wounds with the jaws of ants
lines: He used the mandibles of large ants as clips to hold the edges of a torn intestine, and thread the body absorbs inside it.
know-catgut.caption:
Animal gut had been used as thread before him. What al-Zahrawi set down was its use inside the body, where the thread is absorbed and nothing has to be taken out again. He also described a family whose boys bled to death from small cuts, often read as the earliest clinical account of an inherited bleeding disorder. His warning was blunt: anyone who cuts without knowing anatomy will kill the patient.

know-canon.hook: One medical textbook was taught in Europe for six centuries
know-canon.date: Ibn Sina · Canon of Medicine, c. 1025
lines: Translated at Toledo in the twelfth century, printed in Latin in the 1470s, and still set reading in medical faculties in the sixteenth.
know-canon.caption:
The Canon is five books: principles, some eight hundred simple drugs, diseases organ by organ, diseases of the whole body, and a formulary. Its success was organisation: a physician could find the passage he needed, which made it teachable. That was also the trouble with it. A book good enough to be the syllabus is a book people stop testing, and physicians from Ibn al-Nafis onward had to argue against it.

In 931 a man in Baghdad died through a practitioner's mistake, and al-Muqtadir ordered the examinations. Those who failed were barred, with exemptions for physicians of established reputation. Sinan also arranged for doctors to visit prisons and sent staffed dispensaries out to the villages. The account is a later one and the round number is a round number, but the principle is clear: a licence to practise, granted by examination.

know-free-hospital.hook: Treatment in a medieval Muslim hospital was free
lines: A donor signed over shops, farms or a bathhouse, and the rent paid the staff and the drugs from then on: the endowment said so.
know-free-hospital.caption:
The bimaristan, from a Persian word meaning place of the sick, was funded by waqf, a permanent endowment. The Adudi hospital in Baghdad opened around 981 and Nur al-Din's in Damascus in 1154, with wards divided by complaint, including for mental illness, salaried physicians, surgeons, pharmacists, a kitchen and a library. The system depended on wealthy people wanting a charity that outlived them.

know-rainbow.hook: He built a glass raindrop to explain the rainbow

He was working through Ibn al-Haytham's Optics and reached the rainbow. Rather than argue about it he built a model. The fainter outer bow, he found, comes from an extra reflection, which is also why its colours run the other way. At almost the same time Theodoric of Freiberg in Germany reached the same conclusion by the same kind of experiment; there is no sign either knew of the other.

know-columbus.caption:
Al-Farghani's introduction to astronomy, thirty short chapters with almost no mathematics, was the standard textbook for seven hundred years and where Dante took his figures for the size of the heavens. It carried al-Ma'mun's measurement of the earth. Read with the wrong mile, it put Asia correspondingly nearer. How much was error and how much was wishful thinking is still argued.

know-cairo-1924.caption:
The Egyptian government wanted a reliable printed Qur'an for state schools, where the copies in use were full of errors. The edition follows the reading of Hafs from Asim, uses the Kufan way of dividing and numbering the verses, and fixes the pause marks and the spelling. It was not a new text. It was a decision about which inherited conventions to print, and Sunni and Shia publishers alike follow it.
